title: Thunder, rain and growing things are the work of providence
source_text: Οἴεται γὰρ πρῶτον μὲν μὴ ἔργα θεοῦ εἶναι βροντὰς καὶ ἀστραπὰς καὶ ὑετοὺς. ἤδη σαφέστερον Ἐπικουρίζων· δεύτερον δέ φησιν ὅτι. εἰ καὶ διδῴη τις ταῦτα ἔργα εἶναι θεοῦ, οὐ μᾶλλον ἡμῖν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ταῦτα γίνεται πρὸς τροφὴν ἢ τοῖς φυτοῖς δένδροις τε καὶ πόαις καὶ ἀκάνθαις. συντυχικῶς διδοὺς καὶ οὐ κατὰ πρόνοιαν ὡς ἀληθῶς Ἐπικούρειος ταῦτα συμβαίνειν. εἰ γὰρ οὐ μᾶλλον ἡμῖν ἢ φυτοῖς καὶ δένδροις καὶ πόαις καὶ ἀκάνθαις ταῦτ᾿ ἐστι χρήσιμα, δῆλον ὅτι οὐδ᾿ ἀπὸ προνοίας ταῦτ᾿ ἔρχεται ἢ ἀπὸ προνοίας οὐ μᾶλλον ἡμῶν προνοουμένης ἢ δένδρων καὶ πόας καὶ ἀκάνθης. ἑκάτερον δ᾿ αὐτόθεν ἀσεβὲς. καὶ τὸ τοῖς τοιούτοις ἀντιλέγειν ἱστάμενον πρὸς τὸν ἀσέβειαν ἡμῶν κατηγοροῦντα εὔηθες· παντὶ γὰρ δῆλον ἐκ τῶν εἰρημένων, τίς ὁ ἀσεβής. εἶτά φησιν ὅτι κἂν ταῦτα λέγῃς ἀνθρώποις φύεσθαι (δῆλον δ᾿ ὅτι τὰ φυτὰ καὶ δένδρα καὶ πόας καὶ ἀκάνθας). τί μᾶλλον αὐτὰ ἀνθρώποις φήσεις φύεσθαι ἢ τοῖς ἀλόγοις ζῴοις τοῖς ἀγριωτάτοις; σαφῶς οὖν λεγέτω ὁ Κέλσος ὅτι ἡ τοσαύτη τῶν ἐπὶ γῆς φυομένων διαφορὰ οὐ προνοίας ἐστὶν ἔργον. ἀλλὰ συντυχία τις ἀτόμων τὰς τοσαύτας ποιότητας πεποίηκε, καὶ κατὰ συντυχίαν τοσαῦτα εἴδη φυτῶν καὶ δένδρων καὶ πόας παραπλήσιά ἐστιν ἀλλήλοις. καὶ ὅτι οὐδεὶς λόγος τεχνικὸς ὑπέστησεν αὐτὰ, οὐδ᾿ ἀπὸ νοῦ ἔχει τὴν ἀρχὴν. πάντα θαυμασμὸν ὑπερβεβηκότος. ἀλλ᾿ ἡμεῖς οἱ τῷ ταῦτα κτίσαντι μόνῳ ἀνακείμενοι θεῷ Χριστιανοὶ καὶ ἐπὶ τούτοις χάριν οἴδαμεν τῷ καὶ τούτων δημιουργῷ, ὅτι ἡμῖν τηλικαύτην ἑστίαν εὐτρέπισε καὶ δι᾿ ἡμᾶς τοῖς δουλεύουσιν ἡμῖν ζῴοις· „ὁ ἐξανατέλλων χόρτον τοῖς κτήνεσι καὶ χλόην τῇ δουλείᾳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, (τοῦ) ἐξαγαγεῖν ἄρτον ἐκ τῆς γῆς, καὶ ἵν᾿ οἶνος εὐφραίνῃ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου, καὶ ἱλαρύνηται πρόσωπον ἐν ἐλαίῳ. καὶ ἄρτος στηρίζῃ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου.“ εἰ δὲ καὶ τοῖς ἀγριωτάτοις τῶν ζῴων τροφὰς κατεσκεύασεν, οὐδὲν θαυμαστόν· καὶ ταῦτα γὰρ τὰ ζῷα καὶ ἄλλοι τῶν φιλοσοφησάντων εἰρήκασι γυμνασίου ἕνεκα γεγονέναι τῷ λογικῷ ζῴῳ. φησὶ δέ που τῶν καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς τις σοφῶν· „μὴ εἴπῃς· τί τοῦτο, εἰς τί τοῦτο; πάντα γὰρ εἰς χρείαν αὐτῶν ἔκτισται“ καὶ „μὴ εἴπῃς· τί τοῦτο, εἰς τί τοῦτο; πάντα γὰρ ἐν καιρῷ αὐτῶν ζητηθήσεται.“
pass_a_gloss: For he thinks first that thunders (βρονταί) and lightnings (ἀστραπαί) and rains (ὑετοί) are not works (ἔργα) of God, already more clearly Epicureanizing (Ἐπικουρίζω); and second he says that, even if one should grant (δίδωμι) these to be works of God, not more for us men do these come to be for food than for plants, trees and grasses and thorns, granting like a true Epicurean (Ἐπικούρειος) that these things happen (συμβαίνω) by chance (συντυχικῶς) and not according to providence. For if these are not more useful (χρήσιμα) to us than to plants and trees and grasses and thorns, it is clear that they do not come from providence, or from a providence not taking care more of us than of trees and grass and thorn. Either (ἑκάτερον) is impious (ἀσεβής) straight off (αὐτόθεν); and to speak against (ἀντιλέγω) such things, standing up against one who accuses us of impiety (ἀσέβεια), is silly (εὐήθης); for it is clear to all from the things said who is the impious one. — Then he says that: Even if you say these grow (φύομαι) for men (clearly the plants and trees and grasses and thorns), why will you say that they grow for men rather than for the most savage (ἀγριώτατα) irrational animals? — Let Celsus then say clearly that so great a difference (διαφορά) of things growing on earth is not a work of providence, but a certain chance meeting (συντυχία) of atoms (ἄτομοι) has made so many qualities (ποιότητες), and by chance so many kinds (εἴδη) of plants and trees and grass are similar (παραπλήσια) to one another; and that no craftsmanlike reason (λόγος τεχνικός) gave them substance (ὑφίστημι), nor do they have their beginning (ἀρχή) from a mind (νοῦς) that has surpassed all wonder (θαυμασμός). — But we Christians, devoted (ἀνάκειμαι) only (μόνῳ) to the God who created (κτίζω) these, know thanks (χάριν οἶδα) also for these to the craftsman (δημιουργός) of these too, that he prepared (εὐτρεπίζω) for us so great a home/hearth (ἑστία), and through us for the animals serving (δουλεύω) us: He who makes spring up (ἐξανατέλλω) grass (χόρτος) for the cattle (κτήνη) and green herb (χλόη) for the service (δουλεία) of men, to bring forth bread from the earth, and that wine may gladden (εὐφραίνω) the heart of man, and that the face be made cheerful (ἱλαρύνω) with oil (ἔλαιον), and bread strengthen (στηρίζω) the heart of man. — And if he prepared foods also for the most savage of animals, nothing wondrous; for others also of those who philosophized have said that these animals came to be for the sake of exercise (γυμνάσιον) for the rational animal. And one of the wise (σοφοί) among us says somewhere: Do not say, What is this, for what is this? For all things have been created for their use (χρεία); and: Do not say, What is this, for what is this? For all things will be sought (ζητέω) in their time (καιρός).
pass_b_english: For first he thinks that thunders and lightnings and rains are not works of God, and here he is already showing himself an Epicurean more openly. Second, he says that even if one should grant that these are works of God, they are produced no more as food for us human beings than for plants, for trees and grasses and thorns. In this, like a true Epicurean, he grants that these things happen by chance and not by providence. For if these things are no more useful to us than to plants and trees and grasses and thorns, it is plain either that they do not come from providence at all, or that they come from a providence that takes no more thought for us than for trees and grass and thorn. Each of these is impious on its face; and to take a stand and argue against such things in reply to a man who accuses us of impiety is foolish, for it is plain to everyone from what has been said who the impious one is.

Then he says: “Even if you say that these things grow for human beings” (he plainly means the plants and trees and grasses and thorns), “why will you say that they grow for human beings rather than for the most savage irrational animals?” Let Celsus, then, say plainly that the great variety of the things that grow on the earth is not the work of providence, but that some chance meeting of atoms made such a great range of qualities, and that it is by chance that so many kinds of plants and trees and grass are like one another; and that no craftsman’s reason gave them their being, nor do they have their origin from a Mind that surpasses all wonder.

But we Christians, who are devoted to the God who created these things, and to Him alone, give thanks for these things too to Him who fashioned them as well, because He has made ready for us so great a home, and for our sake for the animals that serve us: “He makes grass spring up for the cattle, and green plants for the service of men, to bring forth bread from the earth, and that wine may gladden the heart of man, that his face may shine with oil, and that bread may strengthen the heart of man” (Psalm 104:14–15).

And if He has prepared food even for the most savage of the animals, it is no wonder; for others too among those who have pursued philosophy have said that these animals also came into being to give exercise to the rational animal. And one of the wise men among us says somewhere: “Do not say, ‘What is this? What is this for?’ For all things have been created for their use” (Sirach 39:21); and, “Do not say, ‘What is this? What is this for?’ For all things will be sought out in their time” (Sirach 39:17).

choices.choice: removed doubled ‘plainly … on its face’ for αὐτόθεν
μόνῳ … θεῷ: ‘devoted to the God who created these things, and to Him alone’ (was ‘the only God’)

Celsus’s words: “Even if you say … most savage irrational animals?”; the earlier points (thunder not God’s work; no more for us than for plants) are Origen’s report of him and kept as report. Origen’s parenthesis (δῆλον δ᾿ ὅτι …) kept inside parentheses within the quotation. Psalm 104:14–15 is LXX Psalm 103:14–15; Origen’s wording differs slightly from the LXX (ἵν᾿ … εὐφραίνῃ, ἱλαρύνηται, στηρίζῃ for indicative/infinitive forms); the editorial (τοῦ) before ἐξαγαγεῖν is followed. The two sayings of ‘one of our wise men’ are Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 39:21 and 39:17 in the Greek numbering; some English Bibles number the second at 39:16–17. Sirach has ‘No one can say’ (οὐκ ἔστιν εἰπεῖν) where Origen reads ‘Do not say’ (μὴ εἴπῃς); his wording is translated. ‘Others among the philosophers’ who said wild beasts exist to exercise the rational animal are not named (presumably Stoics); no source added. ἑστία (‘hearth, home’) rendered ‘home’. Reviewer: μόνῳ goes with θεῷ as the object of devotion (‘devoted to Him alone’), not as a predicate ‘the only God’.
